title: Personal data; husband and family; teaching career
description: Lillian Yangel gives her birth date, parents, and brother, and describes her husband Lester's 35 years with Potlatch. She recounts her year at university, normal school in Vancouver, and teaching primary grades and substituting during the war around Elk River, Troy, and Bovill.

title: Homemaking; drugstore work; clubs and volunteering
description: She says she enjoys cooking and homemaking, worked in the family drugstore from childhood, and helped cook for a forest fire crew. She lists her extension club, Red Cross, and Girl Scout involvement and the 25-year Red Cross pin and wartime commendations she received.

title: Wartime aircraft watch
description: She describes serving on the civilian aircraft ground observer watch during World War Two, taking scheduled shifts, calling in sightings, and how the program ended as planes became too fast to report usefully.

title: Rural versus city life
description: She praises rural neighborliness, where people watch each other's property, and describes the motel community in Arizona that felt like a small town. She weighs city conveniences against her own small-town upbringing and compares her life with friends in large cities.

title: Young people then and now
description: She says today's young people have more free time but less of the self-discipline that early work taught her generation. She believes children then depended on their own resources for entertainment and got more out of it.

title: Childhood recreation; church and school activities
description: She recalls hiking to friends' houses, sunrise breakfasts, swimming, Sunday picnics, winter potlucks, and dances at her family's home with its hardwood floor. She describes an active church choir, junior choir, and school band that kept young people busy.

title: Courtship; marriage; women and work
description: She tells how she met her husband, courted for seven or eight months, and married in Elk River. She discusses earning eighty dollars a month teaching, the expectation that married women stopped working, and how wartime need brought women back into jobs.

title: Adjusting to marriage; company town medical care
description: She says married life held no big surprises, just the usual give and take of living closely with another person. She notes Elk River now has no medical facilities and explains that the Potlatch Lumber Company once ran the hospital for workers and their families.

title: A young woman's future; retirement recreation
description: Reflecting on a young woman's future, she contrasts her own limited childhood communications with a world now at everyone's doorstep. She discusses wintering in Arizona, mushroom picking, television and reading preferences, and camp life.

title: Financial security; childlessness; travel values
description: She considers what would happen if her husband died and how she has grown resigned to such worries. She says she never regretted having no children because she helped raise her brother's, and explains that her family saved money deliberately so they could travel.

title: Depression and war years; hoboes; safety
description: She compares Depression-era scarcity with wartime rationing, noting everyone in a small town shared hard times alike. She recalls unemployed men, many of them lumberjacks, politely asking for food at her back door, and discusses feeling safe then versus locking doors now.

title: Shopping trips; church involvement; childhood outings
description: She describes weekly trips to Moscow for shopping and doctors and her reduced but continuing church activity in Idaho and Arizona. She recalls childhood fairs and school outings, including a car accident in which the superintendent's car overturned and she was knocked out.

title: Table manners; parties and entertaining
description: She contrasts the strict table manners of her childhood with children's freedom today. She describes her mother's bridge club parties with crepe paper flowers, fine china and silverware, from-scratch cooking without refrigeration, and how Depression-era gatherings became simpler but continued.

title: Postwar social life; clubs and cars; gasoline costs
description: The interviewee recalls entertaining, car clubs, and PTA activity around Elk River and Moscow after the Second World War. She talks about more people acquiring cars and how expensive gasoline might change habits again.

title: Decisions with her husband; staying in Boulder
description: She describes how she and her husband talked over big decisions together. She explains they lived in Boulder because of her husband's work, kept their home there, and never found anywhere they preferred.

title: Women's movement; teaching children to work
description: She gives her view that the women's movement is sometimes carried too far but that choices should be up to the individual, and says she never faced discrimination herself. She then argues that work is how children learn responsibility and character before adulthood.

title: Depression-era thrift; credit, savings, and government reliance
description: She contrasts her generation's Depression-taught habits of saving and avoiding credit with younger people's reliance on credit cards, Social Security, and welfare. She says older people keep a reserve for illness or old age while younger ones count on the government.

title: Closing the interview; photographs and archive
description: The interviewer wraps up the questions and arranges for a photograph. She explains that the recording will be kept in the archive for research and goes over the release form and restrictions.
